threads.thread_goal: Align on current pain points and prioritise focus areas for the refresh.

messages.text: Morning all, kicking off the in-store refresh for our project_title. To get started, can we list the main customer issues we see on the floor and at the counter? This will feed straight into T1 and the Customer Questions and Issues Log in A1. Off the top of my head I see a lot of confusion around sizing, where to find specific brands, and refund rules. Also, please call out which aisle you think feels the most crowded or confusing so we can pick one pilot area for layout work linked to T8. Share quick bullets from your last few shifts.

From the last week on late shifts, the top questions I keep getting are:  - Where are the promo items from the leaflet, especially in the household aisle  - Do we have more sizes in the back for basic clothing  - How refunds work when they paid by card vs cash I have started jotting these into A1 for T1, grouped roughly into finding products, stock availability, and refunds. For aisles, the household cleaning aisle feels the most congested and people often stop and look around unsure where to go.

On early mornings I see a lot of questions about:  - Price differences between shelf and till when labels are old  - Where batteries and small accessories are  - If we can hold items until later in the day I agree on the household cleaning aisle, but I would also add the snacks and drinks aisle. It gets very busy and the layout mixes single items with multipacks, so people keep asking where the bigger packs are.

From the counter side, the most frequent issues I note are:  - Returns without receipt, especially small household items  - Exchanges for wrong size in clothing  - Complaints when an item on display is out of stock in the size or colour they want I can help add these into A1 for T1 as a separate group for counter interactions. For aisles, I also hear a lot of people asking where to find basic kitchenware, so that aisle might be another candidate.

Adding from mid-day shifts:  - People struggle to compare similar products, especially cleaning sprays vs refills vs concentrates  - Many ask what is suitable for allergies or sensitive skin in personal care  - Some confusion about multi-buy offers not being clearly signed I think for a pilot aisle we should pick one where we can really improve clarity. Household cleaning or personal care both fit that. Household cleaning might link better to T8 since there are many products that need clearer information on the shelf.

Thanks all, this is helpful. I will start grouping what you shared into themes in A1 for T1:  1. Finding products and signage (where items are, promo items, batteries, kitchenware)  2. Stock and sizing (more sizes in back, out-of-stock on display)  3. Price and offers (label mismatches, multi-buy clarity)  4. Refunds and exchanges (with or without receipt, payment method)  5. Product understanding (how to use, allergies, which pack size) Does this feel like the right grouping, or are we missing anything big before we lock the top issues?

The grouping looks right to me. One more thing I hear is customers not knowing who to ask when they need help, especially in the busier aisles. Maybe that sits under finding products and signage, but we could call it visibility of staff or guidance. For the top issues to tackle first, I would vote for:  - Finding products and signage  - Product understanding  - Refunds and exchanges These seem to cause the most back-and-forth and longer queues.

Agree with the themes. For me the biggest pain on the floor is when shelves look full but the key items are hidden or mixed, so customers cannot spot them quickly. That links to finding products and product understanding together. I would pick:  - Finding products and signage  - Stock and sizing  - Product understanding Refunds and exchanges are important but maybe we can handle those with a quick guide later while we focus first on the aisles.

From the counter view, refunds and exchanges really slow us down, especially when people are unsure of the rules. But I see the point about the aisles. Maybe our top three could be:  - Finding products and signage  - Product understanding  - Refunds and exchanges That way we cover both the floor and the counter. Stock and sizing might improve once we have a clearer stock rotation plan later.

I am aligned with the three that keep coming up: finding products and signage, product understanding, and refunds and exchanges. They also match well with the deliverables we need later, like scripts and checklists. For the pilot aisle, I still think household cleaning is the best candidate:  - High traffic  - Lots of similar products that confuse people  - Many items that could use clearer shelf information for T8 Personal care is also busy, but cleaning feels more chaotic right now.

Sounds like we are converging. To check:  - Top three issues to address first: finding products and signage, product understanding, refunds and exchanges  - Candidate pilot aisles: household cleaning, snacks and drinks, personal care Can you react in this thread if you disagree with that top three, otherwise I will record it as our focus for D1. Then we can narrow down to one pilot aisle for D2.

No objections from me on the top three. For the pilot aisle, I would vote for household cleaning. It is messy to navigate, and we can test clearer groupings and shelf info there that later apply to other aisles. Snacks and drinks are busy but more straightforward, and personal care might need more policy checks for claims, which could slow us down.

I am ok with the top three issues. On the pilot aisle, I still see a lot of confusion in snacks and drinks, but I agree that household cleaning has more potential for clearer information and layout changes. I am fine if we choose household cleaning as long as we keep snacks and drinks in mind for a second wave.

Top three issues work for me. For the pilot aisle, I support household cleaning as well. It is close to the front, so we can easily observe customer behaviour later for T12, and it links strongly to T8 since many products there need clearer shelf information.
Agree on both: the three issues and household cleaning as the pilot aisle. Once we tidy that up and see results, we can reuse the approach for snacks and drinks and personal care.

Thanks for confirming. I will record that:  - For D1, our top three customer pain points to address first are finding products and signage, product understanding, and refunds and exchanges.  - For D2, our pilot area will be the household cleaning aisle. I will update A1 under T1 with these priorities and flag household cleaning as the focus for T8 and T4 later.

I will start adding more detailed examples of questions into A1 for T1 from tonight and tomorrow shifts, especially around product understanding in the household cleaning aisle, so we have a solid base for scripts in the next thread.
I will focus on capturing refund and exchange questions at the counter into A1 for T1 over the next couple of days, so we can later build a clear quick guide and keep queues moving.

threads.thread_goal: Define customer guidance prompts and service scripts for key categories.

messages.text: Picking up from A1 and T1, we now need to draft customer guidance prompts for the top categories under T2. Main focus: household cleaning, personal care, snacks and drinks, basic clothing, and refunds at the counter. I have pulled the most frequent questions from A1 into a rough list. Can we start suggesting opening questions and example recommendations for each category, so we can later compile them into A2 and a quick guide for T5?

For household cleaning under T2, here are some opening questions:  - What type of surface are you cleaning most often  - Do you prefer sprays, wipes, or refills  - Do you need something suitable for allergies or sensitive skin Example recommendations:  - If they mention a busy family kitchen, suggest a multi-surface spray plus wipes for quick spills.  - If they want eco options, guide them to concentrates and refills with clear icons. I will add these into A2 for the household cleaning section.

For snacks and drinks, some opening questions could be:  - Are you looking for single snacks or bigger packs for home  - Any dietary preferences we should keep in mind, like low sugar or vegan  - Is this for everyday use or a special occasion Example recommendations:  - For lunchbox snacks, point to multipacks of bars or crisps.  - For movie night, suggest sharing bags plus drinks on promotion. I can log these in A2 as well.

For basic clothing, opening questions:  - Who is the item for and what is it mainly for, work, school, casual  - Do you prefer a looser or closer fit  - Do you have a budget in mind Example recommendations:  - If they want school basics, show multi-pack t-shirts and socks in the right size range.  - If they are unsure on size, suggest trying two sizes and explain our exchange options briefly. I will add these to A2 under clothing.

For personal care, we need to be careful to stay within company policies and not make medical claims. Opening questions:  - Do you have any known allergies or sensitivities  - Are you looking for everyday use or a specific concern like dry skin  - Do you prefer fragrance-free or scented Example recommendations:  - For sensitive skin, guide to fragrance-free and hypoallergenic ranges, and remind them to read the label.  - For everyday use, suggest value packs in the mid-price range. I will draft this in A2 and later check with the store manager for policy alignment under T2.

On refunds and exchanges for T5, based on A1, a simple prompt at the counter could be:  - Can I check how you paid and if you have the receipt with you Then we can follow a quick path:  - With receipt and within time frame: process standard refund or exchange.  - Without receipt: offer exchange or credit according to policy, and explain clearly. I can start a draft for T5 that lists these steps and some standard phrases, and we can later have the customer service supervisor review it.

These are strong starts. To make sure we meet T2, we need 3 to 5 opening questions and 2 to 3 recommendation examples per category. So far we have that for household cleaning, snacks and drinks, clothing, and personal care. Could each of you add one more example recommendation where you see gaps, especially for edge cases like eco options or budget shoppers, and then we can pull everything into A2 as a first version.

For household cleaning, another recommendation example:  - If a customer lives in a small flat and worries about storage, suggest concentrated products and refills plus one reusable spray bottle. I will add this into A2 and mark it clearly under household cleaning.

For snacks and drinks, another example:  - If they want something for work breaks and mention watching sugar, guide them to nuts, seeds, and low-sugar bars, and show multipacks if they want better value. I will update A2 with this.

For clothing, another example:  - If a customer is unsure about size and comfort for long shifts at work, suggest trying a breathable fabric option and explain that they can exchange within the usual time frame if it does not feel right after a day. I will add this to A2 under clothing.

For personal care, another example:  - If they are shopping for a guest and unsure what to pick, suggest a neutral, mid-range brand with a simple formula and no strong fragrance, and remind them to keep the receipt in case the guest prefers a different product. I will add this into A2 and keep the wording neutral to stay within policy.

On the refunds and exchanges prompts for T5, I like the simple path you suggested. To keep it consistent, maybe we can add one more standard phrase for when we cannot offer a full refund, so staff do not improvise. Could you add that into the T5 draft and then we will send it to the customer service supervisor for a quick policy check before we use it on the floor

Good point. I will add a phrase like:  - In this case I can offer an exchange or store credit according to our policy, would that work for you I will put this into the T5 draft and then share it for review.

We also need to agree how strictly we expect everyone to follow these prompts once A2 is ready. My suggestion for D4 is: treat them as prompts and examples, not word-for-word scripts. That means:  - Always start with at least one opening question from the list to understand needs.  - Then adapt the wording to your own style, as long as you stay within policy and the intent of the guidance. Does anyone see issues with that approach

I like that approach. If we had to follow exact wording, it might feel unnatural and slow us down. Using A2 as prompts with at least one opening question per interaction sounds practical. Maybe we can also add a short note in A2 reminding staff to keep it short during peak times.

Agree, prompts not scripts. In busy aisles I often only have time for one quick question and one suggestion. As long as we are consistent on the questions we ask, it should still improve the experience.
From the counter side, I also prefer prompts. Some customers are in a hurry or upset, so we need flexibility to adjust tone. As long as we cover the key points from A2 and T5, I think that is enough.
No issues from me. I will also check that the personal care prompts in A2 stay within company policies before we finalise, then we can ask the store manager to sign off T2 as done.

Great, sounds like we are aligned. For D3, I will compile all the prompts and examples you shared into A2 as the first version for the five categories and share it with the store manager for a quick check against policy under T2. For D4, we agree that staff should use the prompts as guidance: ask at least one opening question from the list, then adapt wording to the situation while staying within policy. I will note this at the top of A2 so it is clear.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on the daily shelf presentation checklist and pilot aisle layout.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the daily shelf presentation and cleanliness checklist in A3 for T3, plus a simple layout idea for the household cleaning aisle in A4 for T4. The checklist covers facing, gaps, price labels, and cleanliness, and should take under 10 minutes per aisle. The layout proposal groups products by use, like kitchen, bathroom, floors, and eco options. Can you review and comment on what feels realistic during normal shifts, and what might slow us down

On early shifts I usually have time to walk each aisle. The A3 checklist looks doable if we keep it tight. I like the order: 1) facing, 2) gaps, 3) price labels, 4) cleanliness. One suggestion: add a quick tick box for damaged packaging so we can pull those items aside. For the A4 layout, grouping by use makes sense. We just need to make sure the top sellers stay at eye level and that refills are close to the main products.

From late shifts, the 10 minutes per aisle for T3 feels tight but possible if we split aisles between us. Maybe we can mark in A3 which items are must-do every day and which can be done every other day when it is very busy. For the household cleaning layout in A4, I like the idea of a clear eco section with simple signage. Could we also add a small sign at the start of the aisle explaining the grouping, like kitchen cleaners first, then bathroom, then floors

From the counter, I see the impact when price labels are wrong or missing. In A3, can we make price label checks a clear separate line, maybe with a note to flag any mismatches to the shift lead immediately. For the A4 layout, I would just ask that we keep some of the most common items near the front of the aisle so customers can grab them quickly without walking all the way down when they are in a rush.

Thanks for drafting these. To keep T3 under 10 minutes per aisle, I suggest we structure A3 as:  - Top row: facing and gaps, quick visual scan.  - Middle row: price labels and promo tags.  - Bottom row: cleanliness and damaged items. We can also add a small space to note any low-stock items to feed into T9 later. On A4, I like the grouping by use and the eco section. We should also mark where we want to place the top 10 products from T8 so they are easy to spot.

Good points. I will update A3 to add a damaged packaging tick box and make price labels a separate line with a note to flag mismatches. I will also adjust A4 to keep top sellers at eye level and place refills next to the main products. Once updated, we can test the checklist on one shift to meet the T3 definition of done.

I can run a quick test of the updated A3 checklist on tonight's shift in two aisles, including household cleaning, and time how long it takes. I will note any steps that feel slow and share feedback so we can tweak before we sign off D5.

I can also try the checklist on the morning shift tomorrow in a different aisle and see if the 10-minute target holds when we are filling shelves at the same time. I will pay attention to whether the order of checks matches how we naturally move through the aisle.

I like the idea of noting low-stock items on A3. That will help when we set up T9 later. Maybe we can add a simple column for 'needs top-up' so whoever does the checklist can quickly mark it without writing long notes.
Agreed. I will add a 'needs top-up' column to A3 and keep it as a simple tick. That should keep T3 within the time limit while giving us better visibility for stock checks.

Once we have tonight and tomorrow's tests of A3, can you both share a quick summary here: how long it took per aisle and any steps you skipped or combined. If it looks good, we can confirm D5 and start using the checklist in all aisles.

Quick update from tonight: I tested A3 in the household cleaning aisle and one grocery aisle. It took about 8 minutes per aisle when I focused only on the checklist. The order felt natural: facing and gaps first, then labels, then cleanliness and damaged items. The 'needs top-up' column was easy to tick. I did not feel the need to skip any steps.

Morning test done: I used A3 in two aisles while also topping up stock. It took closer to 10 minutes per aisle, but still manageable. I did facing and gaps as I filled, then a quick pass for labels and cleanliness. I think it is realistic for daily use as long as we share aisles between us.

Thanks for testing. Based on your feedback, I suggest we confirm A3 as our standard checklist for all aisles for D5. It meets the T3 criteria and fits within normal shifts. For the pilot layout in A4 for T4, are there any strong objections to starting in the household cleaning aisle next Monday If not, I will record D6 with that start date and ask the store manager or visual merchandiser to sign off the layout.

No objections from me. Monday works well, and we can adjust the layout during quieter moments that day without extra staffing. I will prepare a simple sketch from A4 to show the store manager for sign-off under T4.
Monday start is fine for me. I am on the late shift, so I can help tidy the new layout and watch how customers move through the aisle for T12 later.
No issues from the counter side. Once the new layout is in place, I will pay attention to whether we get fewer 'where is this cleaner' questions and note that for T12.

Great, I will record that:  - For D5, A3 is approved as the daily shelf presentation and cleanliness checklist for all aisles.  - For D6, the pilot layout in A4 for the household cleaning aisle is approved to start next Monday, pending store manager or visual merchandiser sign-off under T4. I will update A3 and A4 with these notes so everyone is clear.

threads.thread_goal: Set routines for follow-up, stock checks, and weekly huddles.

messages.text: Now that we have prompts and the pilot layout, we need to agree on routines for follow-up, stock checks, and weekly huddles. I have drafted:  - A simple follow-up flow for special orders under T6, to go into A5.  - A weekly 10-minute huddle format for T7, to be summarised in A6.  - A first pass at a stock check rotation plan for T9, to be tracked in A7. Can we review these and decide who leads the huddles on each shift for D7, and which areas we prioritise in the stock rotation for D8

On special orders for T6, the draft flow in A5 looks clear: order placement, confirmation, update if delayed, and reminder before pickup. I would add one more standard phrase for delays, like: 'We are still waiting for your item to arrive, we expect it by [day], and we will let you know as soon as it is ready.' I can help test this with a few recent special orders and note how customers respond.

For the stock rotation plan in A7 under T9, I agree with focusing on high-loss and high-demand areas first. I would list:  - Household cleaning  - Snacks and drinks  - Personal care  - Basic clothing accessories We can rotate checks by day and shift, for example: morning checks snacks and drinks on Mon and Wed, household cleaning on Tue and Thu, and late shifts cover personal care and clothing on alternating days.

On the weekly huddle format in A6 for T7, I like the simple agenda: wins, issues, quick fixes. For timing, could we set:  - Morning shift: 10 minutes after opening, once the first rush is over.  - Mid shift: just before the lunch peak.  - Late shift: 30 minutes before closing. We should also decide who leads each huddle so it actually happens and notes are posted.

For T10, I started a list of best practices for preventing shoplifting while keeping good service. Examples:  - Greet customers as they enter the aisle.  - Stay present in high-risk areas without hovering.  - Offer help if someone seems unsure, rather than watching silently. I will make sure these align with existing loss-prevention rules and then share with the team for acknowledgement.

Those huddle times sound workable. For D7, we need to confirm both the schedule and who leads. My proposal:  - Morning huddle: led by 244639.  - Mid huddle: led by 486724.  - Late huddle: led by 246501. I can capture the format and schedule in A6 under T7. Does anyone see conflicts with these lead roles
I am fine to lead the morning huddle. I am usually in early and can quickly run through wins, issues, and quick fixes, then post a short recap in the channel.
Happy to lead the mid huddle. I will keep it tight so we do not run into the lunch peak, and I will make sure any changes to displays or scripts are noted in A6.

I can take the late huddle. It fits well with checking how the day went and planning quick fixes for the next day. I will also highlight any follow-up needed on special orders from T6 or stock issues from A7.

I will help test the T6 follow-up flow in A5 with at least three special orders this week. I will note how many contacts we make and whether customers seem clearer about timing. That should help us refine the standard phrases before we finalise A5.

On D8, we need to agree the priority areas for the stock check rotation in A7 under T9. Based on what you shared, I suggest we lock in:  - Household cleaning  - Snacks and drinks  - Personal care  - Basic clothing accessories And use the rotation you proposed: mornings focus on snacks and drinks plus household cleaning on alternating days, late shifts focus on personal care and clothing. Any other areas we should include at this stage
That list covers the main high-loss and high-demand areas I see. We can always add more later if needed, but starting with these four for T9 makes sense.
Agree with those four areas. I would just note in A7 that if we spot repeated gaps in any other aisle, we can temporarily add it to the rotation for a couple of weeks.
I am fine with that plan. I will update A7 with the rotation by day and shift, and mark the four priority areas clearly so it is easy to follow.

Since everyone is ok with the huddle leads and times, I will record D7 as: weekly 10-minute huddles per shift using the A6 agenda, led by 244639 in the morning, 486724 mid shift, and 246501 late shift. For D8, we confirm the stock check rotation in A7 under T9 focusing on household cleaning, snacks and drinks, personal care, and basic clothing accessories, with the rotation split between morning and late shifts as discussed.

I will also start drafting A6 to include a short onboarding note for T11, summarising the new displays, checklists, scripts, and who to ask for help. Once done, we can ask the store manager to review and approve it.
I will make sure any learnings from special order follow-ups in A5 and T6 are brought into the late huddles so we keep improving the process.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and decide on adjustments before wider rollout.

messages.text: We have now run the new layout in the household cleaning aisle for a few days and collected before-and-after observations in A8 under T12. Before the change, we saw more customers stopping mid-aisle looking around and asking where items were. After the change, more people seem to walk straight to the right section. Let us review the notes in A8 along with A3 and A4 and decide what to adjust before we roll out similar changes elsewhere.

From the morning shifts, I noticed fewer 'where is kitchen cleaner' questions. People seem to understand the grouping better. However, some customers still miss the eco section at the end of the aisle. Maybe we should add a small sign at the start of the aisle pointing out that eco options are grouped together further down.

At the counter, I have heard fewer complaints about not finding the right cleaner, but a couple of customers mentioned that they did not notice the floor cleaners until they were already at the till. Maybe the signage for floor products needs to be a bit clearer or placed slightly higher.

Looking at A8, I see that time spent in the aisle seems a bit shorter on average, and there are fewer signs of visible confusion. One thing I noticed on my shift is that some price labels moved when we changed the layout, and a couple of promos were not aligned. We should double-check A3 is being used after any layout change to catch those quickly.

From my observations in A8, customers now tend to head straight to the right half of the aisle based on their need, which is good. The main issues I still see are:  - Eco section not obvious enough.  - Floor cleaners slightly hidden on the lower shelves.  - Some refills not clearly linked to the main products. I suggest we tweak A4 to move floor cleaners a bit higher and add a small 'eco options ahead' sign at the start of the aisle, plus a simple 'refills here' tag next to the main products.

I agree with those tweaks. On late shifts, I also saw a couple of people walk past the eco section without noticing it. A small sign at the start and maybe a green icon on the shelf edge could help. For refills, placing them directly next to the main product with a small 'refill' label should make the link clearer.

I can help move the floor cleaners up one shelf and adjust the refills placement on my next morning shift. I will also run through A3 afterwards to make sure facing and labels are correct after the change.

Thanks. I will update A4 with the new positions and signage notes so we have a clear record of the adjusted layout. That way, when we reuse the approach in other aisles, we can include the eco and refill signage from the start.

On the price labels, I will remind the team at the counter to flag any mismatches they hear about straight away so the floor team can check A3 for that aisle. That should reduce the number of customers who feel misled by promo tags.

In terms of customer behaviour from A8, I also noticed that people ask fewer basic 'where is' questions but more specific ones like 'which one is better for pets' or 'which is more eco'. That suggests the layout is working and we can now lean more on the prompts in A2 to guide choices.

That is a good sign. It means the layout and A3 are doing their job, and we can focus on better conversations using A2. Before we roll out similar layouts to other aisles, I suggest we:  - Finalise the tweaks to A4 for household cleaning.  - Capture a short summary of what worked and what we changed in A8.  - Use that to brief the team in the next weekly huddles via A6.

I can write a short summary in A8 highlighting:  - Fewer basic location questions.  - Slightly shorter time in aisle.  - Need for clearer eco and floor cleaner signage. Then we can share that summary in the next huddles using the A6 format.
Once we see a couple more days of behaviour after the tweaks, I can add a few extra notes into A8 from the morning shifts, especially if we notice any new confusion points.

I will keep logging observations for T12 over the next three days after the tweaks, focusing on questions asked, time spent, and any visible confusion. Then we can decide if the layout is ready to copy to snacks and drinks or if we need more changes.

Thanks everyone. No formal decision needed here, but to summarise the pilot:  - The new layout in A4, supported by A3, has reduced basic location questions and visible confusion according to A8.  - We will tweak eco and floor cleaner visibility and tighten the link between main products and refills.  - After three more days of observations under T12, we will decide in the huddles which aisle to tackle next, likely snacks and drinks. I will note this summary in A8 so we have a clear record before wider rollout.
